---
title: Command line
---

Sometimes the question is not in your code at all. You are staring at a bucket listing, or a log line, or a colleague's message, and you want to know what `report.parq` is going to be served as without opening a REPL. The package ships a small console script for exactly that moment.

## Install

Install it as a tool so it is on your path everywhere.

```bash
uv tool install content-types
# or
pipx install content-types
```

Inside a project that already depends on the package the script is on the virtualenv's path, so `uv run content-types ...` works there without a separate install.

## Use

One argument in, one line out.

```bash
content-types example.jpg
# image/jpeg

content-types .webp
# image/webp

content-types data.parquet
# application/vnd.apache.parquet
```

The argument goes straight through `get_content_type()` with its defaults, so the tool inherits the library's manners: case does not matter, a bare extension works with or without the dot, and an unknown extension prints `application/octet-stream` and exits 0. It does the forward lookup only. For the reverse direction, open Python.

## Flags and exit codes

The script is deliberately tiny, so this table is the whole contract.

| Invocation | Output | Exit code |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `content-types NAME` | the content type, or `application/octet-stream` for an unknown extension | 0 |
| `content-types` | usage text on stdout | 1 |
| `content-types -h` or `--help` | usage text | 0 |
| `content-types --version` | the installed package version | 0 |

Extra arguments after the first are ignored. There are no environment variables and no configuration file to discover. Under the hood the script is the function `content_types.cli()` wired up in `pyproject.toml`, which means you can call it yourself if you ever want the same behaviour from inside another tool.
